paras.text: Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is the most powerful tool available for organic structure determination. Like infrared spectroscopy, NMR can be used with a very small amount of sample, and it does not harm the sample. The NMR spectrum provides a great deal of information about the structure of the compound, and many structures can be determined using only the NMR spectrum. More commonly, however, NMR spectroscopy is used in conjunction with other forms of spectroscopy and chemical analysis to determine the structures of complicated organic molecules.

paras.text: In the absence of an external magnetic field, proton magnetic moments have degenerate (of same energy) random orientations. When an external magnetic field is applied, each proton in a sample assumes either low energy alpha-spin (α-spin) state, in which the proton magnetic field is aligned with the applied field, or high energy beta-spin (β-spin) state, which has magnetic field aligned against the applied field. Because the α-spin state is lower in energy, there are more α-spin states than β-spins. In a strong magnetic field, the energy difference between the two spin states is larger than it is in a weaker field. In fact, the energy difference is proportional to the strength of the magnetic field.

paras.text: The nuclear magnetic resonance phenomenon occurs when nuclei aligned with an applied field are induced to absorb energy and change their spin orientation with respect to the applied field. The energy of absorption is a quantized process and the energy absorbed must equal the energy difference between the two spin states involved. A nucleus, when irradiated with radio-frequency photons having energy equal to the energy difference between the two spin states, a proton in the α-spin state can absorb a photon and flip to the β-spin state. The phenomenon is called flipping.   ΔE = Eβ – Eα = hν

24.2.2.3 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy

Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is the most powerful tool available for organic structure determination. Like infrared spectroscopy, NMR can be used with a very small amount of sample, and it does not harm the sample. The NMR spectrum provides a great deal of information about the structure of the compound, and many structures can be determined using only the NMR spectrum. More commonly, however, NMR spectroscopy is used in conjunction with other forms of spectroscopy and chemical analysis to determine the structures of complicated organic molecules.

Nuclear spin and spin flipping

Like electrons, atomic nucleus proton also has the property of spin. Thus, the atomic nuclei behave like tiny magnets, as the spinning charged bodies produce magnetic field. In fact, any atomic nucleus that possesses either odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both has a quantized nuclear spin and a magnetic moment, and can be detected in NMR spectroscopy. Nuclei which have even atomic number and even mass number have zero spin and zero magnetic moment, and are therefore NMR inactive.

NMR is used to study a wide variety of nuclei, including ¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁵N, ¹⁹F, and ³¹P. Organic chemists find proton (¹H) and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR to be most useful because hydrogen and carbon are major components of organic compounds. In this book, we will discuss only the proton NMR (¹H NMR) spectroscopy.

In the absence of an external magnetic field, proton magnetic moments have degenerate (of same energy) random orientations. When an external magnetic field is applied, each proton in a sample assumes either low energy alpha-spin (α-spin) state, in which the proton magnetic field is aligned with the applied field, or high energy beta-spin (β-spin) state, which has magnetic field aligned against the applied field. Because the α-spin state is lower in energy, there are more α-spin states than β-spins. In a strong magnetic field, the energy difference between the two spin states is larger than it is in a weaker field. In fact, the energy difference is proportional to the strength of the magnetic field.

The nuclear magnetic resonance phenomenon occurs when nuclei aligned with an applied field are induced to absorb energy and change their spin orientation with respect to the applied field. The energy of absorption is a quantized process and the energy absorbed must equal the energy difference between the two spin states involved. A nucleus, when irradiated with radio-frequency photons having energy equal to the energy difference between the two spin states, a proton in the α-spin state can absorb a photon and flip to the β-spin state. The phenomenon is called flipping.   ΔE = Eβ – Eα = hν

24.2.2.3 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy

Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is the most powerful tool available for organic structure determination. Like infrared spectroscopy, NMR can be used with a very small amount of sample, and it does not harm the sample. The NMR spectrum provides a great deal of information about the structure of the compound, and many structures can be determined using only the NMR spectrum. More commonly, however, NMR spectroscopy is used in conjunction with other forms of spectroscopy and chemical analysis to determine the structures of complicated organic molecules.

Nuclear spin and spin flipping

Like electrons, atomic nucleus proton also has the property of spin. Thus, the atomic nuclei behave like tiny magnets, as the spinning charged bodies produce magnetic field. In fact, any atomic nucleus that possesses either odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both has a quantized nuclear spin and a magnetic moment, and can be detected in NMR spectroscopy. Nuclei which have even atomic number and even mass number have zero spin and zero magnetic moment, and are therefore NMR inactive.

NMR is used to study a wide variety of nuclei, including ¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁵N, ¹⁹F, and ³¹P. Organic chemists find proton (¹H) and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR to be most useful because hydrogen and carbon are major components of organic compounds. In this book, we will discuss only the proton NMR (¹H NMR) spectroscopy.

In the absence of an external magnetic field, proton magnetic moments have degenerate (of same energy) random orientations. When an external magnetic field is applied, each proton in a sample assumes either low energy alpha-spin (α-spin) state, in which the proton magnetic field is aligned with the applied field, or high energy beta-spin (β-spin) state, which has magnetic field aligned against the applied field. Because the α-spin state is lower in energy, there are more α-spin states than β-spins. In a strong magnetic field, the energy difference between the two spin states is larger than it is in a weaker field. In fact, the energy difference is proportional to the strength of the magnetic field.

Figure 24.8 Nuclear spin states in absence and presence of magnetic field.

The nuclear magnetic resonance phenomenon occurs when nuclei aligned with an applied field are induced to absorb energy and change their spin orientation with respect to the applied field. The energy of absorption is a quantized process and the energy absorbed must equal the energy difference between the two spin states involved. A nucleus, when irradiated with radio-frequency photons having energy equal to the energy difference between the two spin states, a proton in the α-spin state can absorb a photon and flip to the β-spin state. The phenomenon is called flipping. ΔE = Eβ – Eα = hν
